n: Abraham explains that God had given him the Urim and Thummim while he lived in Ur — a sacred instrument used to receive revelation. Through it he will see the heavens.

f.g: Hebrew, often rendered “lights and perfections”; a divinely prepared instrument for revelation (Exodus 28:30; D&C 17:1; Joseph Smith—History 1:35).

n: Abraham sees that the stars are vast, and one of them is nearest to God’s throne, surrounded by other great stars.

f.w: nearest unto the throne of God

n: The Lord calls these the “governing ones.” The greatest, Kolob, is nearest to God and governs all the heavenly bodies of the same order as our earth. The lesson points beyond astronomy to God’s orderly rule.

f.g: Possibly related to the Semitic root qlb, “heart” or “center,” or to kokab, “star.”

n: On Kolob one revolution equals one day of the Lord’s time — a thousand of our years. God’s timescale differs vastly from ours.
The Lord teaches that the moon (“lesser light”) is “above” the earth in its reckoning because its time moves more slowly — its cycles are fewer than earth’s days.

f.g: the counting or measuring of time.

n: God tells Abraham he has seen these facts for himself and is being given to know the “set times” of the earth, sun, and moon — the God-ordained order of time.

f.g: the appointed time or cycle fixed by God.

n: The moon’s cycle is longer in its reckoning than the earth’s daily cycle.

f.w: the set time of the lesser light

n: Where two such levels exist, there will be another above them — a body whose time runs longer still. Abraham is learning a principle of hierarchy.
This ascending order continues body by body until one reaches Kolob, which keeps the Lord’s time and governs all bodies of our order near God’s throne.

f.w: Kolob is set nigh unto the throne of God

n: Abraham is allowed to know the “set time” of all the light-giving stars, up to the throne of God.

f.w: the set time of all the stars

n: Abraham talks with the Lord face to face, as friends talk, and the Lord tells him about His creations.
With tender words — “My son, my son” — the Lord touches Abraham’s eyes, and he sees God’s creations multiply without end. Compare Moses’s similar vision of worlds without number.

f.w: I could not see the end thereof

n: God teaches Abraham names for the heavenly bodies: Shinehah (sun), Kokob (star), Olea (moon), and Kokaubeam (stars). Kokob and Kokaubeam closely resemble Hebrew kokab and kokabim.
At night, under these stars, the Lord promises to multiply Abraham’s descendants beyond counting, like the stars and the sands.
God shows Abraham these things before he enters Egypt so that he can teach them there. Abraham will share this knowledge of the heavens with the Egyptians.
The principle restated: wherever one thing is above another, something greater still exists. Kolob is greatest among the stars Abraham has seen because it is nearest to God.
If the moon is above the earth, another body may be above it. And whatever God sets His heart to do, He will do.

f.w: there is nothing that the Lord thy God shall take in his heart to do but what he will do it

n: Now the lesson moves from stars to spirits: even if one spirit is more intelligent than another, both are eternal — without beginning or end. “Gnolaum” means eternal.
Just as stars rise in greatness, spirits differ in intelligence, and God is more intelligent than them all. This is the key to the whole astronomy lesson.

f.w: I am more intelligent than they all

n: The Lord reminds Abraham that He sent His angel to rescue him from Elkenah’s priest — the God of all the heavens is personally aware of Abraham.

f.w: sent his angel to deliver thee

n: God dwells among all His creations and rules with perfect wisdom over every intelligence. He “came down” to teach Abraham — showing that greatness for God means condescending to lift others.

f.w: I came down in the beginning in the midst of all the intelligences

n: Abraham is shown the spirits (“intelligences”) organized before the world, among whom were many “noble and great ones.”

f.g: Here, the spirits of God’s children in their premortal state.

n: God stands among these good spirits and chooses them as His rulers. He tells Abraham he was one of them, chosen before birth — a teaching known as foreordination.

f.w: thou wast chosen before thou wast born

n: One “like unto God” — the premortal Jesus Christ — proposes to go down and organize an earth from existing materials as a home for these spirits. Creation is organizing, not making from nothing.

f.w: one among them that was like unto God
we will take of these materials

n: The earth’s purpose is a test: to “prove” God’s children and see if they will obey all His commands. Mortality is a school of choice.

f.w: to see if they will do all things

n: Those who keep their “first estate” (premortal life) receive a body and mortal life; those who keep their “second estate” (mortal life) receive glory forever. Each stage of faithfulness leads to more.
God asks, “Whom shall I send?” One like the Son of Man — Christ — answers, “Here am I, send me.” Another (Lucifer) also volunteers, but God chooses the first.

f.w: like unto the Son of Man
f.g: Jesus Christ in His premortal state.

n: The rejected one becomes angry, rebels, and loses his first estate, and many follow him. This is the War in Heaven; Satan and his followers never receive mortal bodies.
